document.note: Armacost and Adamishin seek to limit arms flows under the 'third option'. Armacost insists on symmetry: if the USSR arms Kabul, the US must be able to arm the resistance via Pakistan, and the Soviets must not accuse Pakistan of violations. Adamishin warns this would undercut the Geneva accords; the exchange grows heated.

events.description: Special Working Group on Afghanistan: Armacost and Adamishin discuss Geneva Accords, arms-supply symmetry, and Soviet withdrawal
Shultz and Shevardnadze conversation the night before; Shevardnadze said troop withdrawal would be completed in 1988, half in first three months
UN resolution on Pakistan/Afghan border language later used by Cordovez in Geneva Accords
Soviet-Afghan treaty cited by Adamishin as basis for Soviet arms supply
Armacost and Adamishin negotiate US-Soviet understanding on arms supply, with Soviet three options and US draft agreed minutes.
Armacost reads two draft agreed minutes proposing a three-year mutual restraint or reciprocal supply rights; Adamishin rejects them.
Soviet party leaves to attend inauguration of Nuclear Risk Reduction Center.
Armacost and Adamishin discuss arms supply symmetry, moratorium proposal, and interpretation of Pakistan's obligations under the Geneva accords.
Shevardnadze stated the evening before that the USSR wished Afghanistan to be neutral.
Special Working Group on Afghanistan meeting between Armacost and Adamishin delegations on Geneva accords arms symmetry.
events.place: Under Secretary Armacost's Office, Washington, D.C.

events.description: Shultz and Shevardnadze conversation in which Shevardnadze said Soviet troop withdrawal would be completed in 1988, half in first three months.
UN resolution on Afghanistan, source of the border language later used in the Geneva accords.
Agreed that U.S. representative in Geneva would confirm with Pakistan's representative, and Soviet representative would contact the Afghans, on Cordovez's interim government role.
Special Working Group discussion in which Adamishin and Armacost debated Soviet and US formulas on arms supplies under the Geneva accords.
Armacost read paragraph 8 of Article II of the draft Afghan-Pakistan bilateral agreement on non-interference regarding mercenaries and proposed that the term not apply to the resistance.
Soviet side agreed in Geneva to a nine-month troop withdrawal timetable, with fifty percent withdrawn within three months, and dropped the linkage to a coalition government.
Shevardnadze stated the evening before that the Soviet Union wished Afghanistan to become neutral, with neutrality arrangements to be decided later.
Planned dinner between the two ministers (Shultz and Shevardnadze) that evening to discuss a neutral Afghanistan.
Armacost-Adamishin session on arms-supply formula in the Geneva accords; Adamishin rejects both US variants, calls the Soviet third option maximum position.
Secretary's luncheon during the session break.
Conversation between the ministers (Shultz and Shevardnadze) the night before.
Armacost and Adamishin discuss arms-supply symmetry, Soviet three options, and Pakistani obligations under the Geneva accords.
Adamishin states that the Geneva accords are silent on military assistance and that Soviets would not approve arms supplies to Pakistan or the resistance.
Armacost proposes a moratorium or reciprocal restraint on arms supplies, noting the U.S. cannot expose Pakistan to violation charges.

The two foreign ministers met the night before the working group session; Shevardnadze indicated the Soviets could not accept a unilateral U.S. halt of arms supplies and spoke about Cordovez's role in arranging an interim government.
Armacost and Adamishin discuss the symmetry issue (arms supply moratorium vs. continued supply) obstructing signature of the Geneva accords.

Armacost says the U.S. representative in Geneva would be contacted that morning to confirm with the Pakistani representative the interim-government role for Cordovez; Adamishin says the Soviet representative would also contact the Afghans.
USSR-Afghanistan treaty took effect, cited by Adamishin as basis for Soviet arms supply to Kabul regardless of regime.

Armacost proposes a time-limited, mutual moratorium on arms supplies; Adamishin rejects it and offers three options: unilateral U.S. cessation, U.S. not signing, or an internal understanding to comply only with the accords' text.
Armacost and Adamishin discuss US and Soviet formulas on arms supplies to Afghanistan, the moratorium proposal and the public presentation of the understanding. Matlock participates.
Shevardnadze stated the evening before that the Soviet Union wished Afghanistan to become neutral, which could be incompatible with a military supply relationship.
events.quote: Armacost recalled Shevardnadze statement of the evening before

events.description: Adamishin suggests that the two ministers discuss neutrality and arms at dinner that evening.
Dick Murphy proposed a three-year moratorium on arms supplies to Shevardnadze in Moscow. Shevardnadze did not reply.
Adamishin rejects Armacost's third point on Pakistan. Armacost asks Adamishin to convey the US moratorium proposal to Shevardnadze, who would receive it as a fifth point.
Armacost-Adamishin talks on arms supply to Afghan parties; U.S. proposed a moratorium, Soviets proposed an 'internal understanding' formula.
Armacost read two draft agreed minutes proposing a three-year mutual refraining from military assistance, or freedom to supply if the other side supplied.
Adamishin said both US draft variants would be extremely difficult for the Soviets and amounted to remaking the Geneva accords.
Meeting recessed for half hour; Soviets attended Nuclear Risk Reduction Center inauguration.
Session broke for the Secretary's luncheon, then resumed with Armacost and Adamishin one-on-one, joined by Matlock, Dubinin and Alekseyev.

key_claims: Armacost says symmetry on military assistance is the sole remaining obstacle to concluding the Geneva Accords.
Adamishin states the Soviet Union has taken a firm political decision to withdraw troops within 1988, half in the first three months.
The US proposes either a reciprocal moratorium on arms supplies or reciprocal right with practical means to supply the mujahidin.
The Soviets reject ceasing arms supplies to the Kabul government, citing sovereign rights and the 1921 treaty.
Armacost insists the US must be able to deliver arms across the Pakistan border without Pakistan being accused of violating the Geneva Accords.
The US claims the Soviets are already transferring weaponry in Afghanistan to Kabul ahead of entry into force.
The US sought an arrangement allowing arms to the mujahidin via Pakistan without Soviet charges that Pakistan violated the accords.
Adamishin insisted the Geneva accords were silent on arms supplies and offered only an internal understanding.
Armacost proposed a three-year mutual moratorium on military assistance without prejudice to legal rights.
Adamishin said the Soviets would criticize but not invoke the Geneva accords against US supplies, and could not guarantee ending Soviet arms to Kabul.
The US argued Congress would see a formula as a trick if Pakistan could be accused of violations for transiting aid.
The US sought Soviet acquiescence that continued US arms supplies via Pakistan to the mujahidin would not violate the Geneva accords.
Adamishin refused to guarantee the USSR would not criticize Pakistan as violating the accords, and said the Soviets could not bless US supplies.
Soviet formula: both sides supply at own risk, with criticism allowed but not framed as a Geneva violation.
Armacost proposed a three-year moratorium on arms supplies linked to a broad-based Afghan government; Adamishin called it unacceptable but would convey it.
The USSR conceded a nine-month withdrawal with 50% in three months and dropped linkage to a coalition government.
